analysis.one_liner: Lets the government strip drug monopolies when U.S. prices exceed prices in five other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in two House committees from March 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023, despite 18 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Health and Human Services Department to review brand-name drug prices every year against prices in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan. If a U.S. price is higher than the median abroad, or unreasonable on its own terms, the government would void the drug's exclusive rights, license any company to make a cheaper version, and speed up generic approval. Manufacturers would also have to report their prices, revenues, research spending, and advertising spending each year.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay U.S. prices for brand-name drugs, including people with Medicare, Medicaid, employer insurance, or no insurance; taxpayers who fund Medicare and Medicaid drug purchases; and generic drug makers who could win licenses to make cheaper copies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, taxpayers, and generic drug makers

how_it_helps.text: Requires an annual review of every brand-name drug's price against the median price in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan, with any person able to petition for a review of a specific drug [S2][S3].

For drugs found excessively priced, HHS would void government-granted exclusivity, issue open licenses letting anyone make or import the drug, and speed generic or biosimilar reviews to within 8 months [S2][S3].

Manufacturers would have to report prices, revenues, research costs, and advertising spending, with penalties from 0.5% to 1% of the drug's gross sales for each day a report is late, and a public database would track every determination [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose monopoly profits on excessively priced drugs would end once competitors could make the drug at world-market prices.

drawbacks.text: Eroding patent protections on the most expensive drugs could reduce the reward for developing new medicines, the standard objection the industry and many economists raise to any government override of drug patents [S3].

Foreign prices are set under different government systems, so using them as a benchmark (or the discretionary 'higher than reasonable' fallback) gives HHS broad judgment with little guidance, which manufacturers and courts could contest for years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients on drugs priced far above world levels, the benefit is direct and immediate: competition under license can cut prices sharply. The cost is that some future drug development may be less profitable, and the price benchmarks leave a lot to administrative discretion. On balance the bill transfers money from drug company profits to patients in a targeted way, but it never advanced far enough to be tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and two subcommittees, and neither committee ever took it up, so it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced March 23, 2021 by Rep. Ro Khanna with 18 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
Referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees [S5].

Referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee in March 2021 and the Judiciary antitrust subcommittee in October 2021, with no further action recorded before the Congress ended January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers keep their monopoly pricing without any international benchmark, and their patented profits were never threatened. American patients continue paying U.S. drug prices rather than world prices, and Congress instead enacted narrower drug price policies in 2022 through separate legislation.

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 18 cosponsors

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the referral in March 2021 and never scheduled a markup or hearing, leaving the bill there

against.name: Jerry Nadler
against.what_they_did: His committee held the bill for a joint referral and never took it up beyond an October 2021 subcommittee referral

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Opposed government price benchmarking and patent-override mechanisms throughout this period through lobbying and public campaigns

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans supported the bill; the record shows no Senate sponsor or Republican cosponsor [S4].

industries.note: The bill would end their exclusive rights whenever U.S. prices exceed median prices in five peer countries, and force disclosure of prices, profits, and marketing spending, with per-day fines for late reports. Their interest in keeping monopoly U.S. pricing runs directly against patients who pay it.
Open licenses and 8-month expedited reviews would let them make cheap versions of excessively priced drugs and win new market share. Cheaper copies benefit patients at the same time.
